 Baththa: A feel-good movie that shows the power of second chances
 Published:
 22 Oct 2026
 Modified:
 24 Oct 2026
 Overall, Baththa is a comfort watch from the Kollywood industry whose releases are delivering back-to-back praise from the audience these days.
 Afshin Abdulla
 Baththa is a feel-good Tamil movie directed by Balaji Tharaneetharan starring Vijay Sethupathi. The duo reunites after Seethakaathi which delivered one of Vijay Sethupathi’s best performances ever. 
 Baththa tells the story of a feared gangster and a shy schoolboy who are placed against each other as a gangster played by Vijay Sethupathi gets stuck in a bathroom because of the boy’s innocent mistake, and whose unexpected time in there brings about a change in him. Much like its titular character, Baththa disguises itself as a gangster film, only to reveal a more vulnerable, feel-good side as it delves into the emotional depths of its protagonist. The film shows that it’s not too late to redeem yourself.  
 The movie introduces the titular character Baththa played by Vijay Sethupathi as an invincible and ruthless gangster. The 80s Madras setting provides a perfect stage for Baththa's mythic introduction. He’s presented as an urban legend and his invincibility is brought to the audience through a comic book aesthetic where the school children share to each other their own imagination of a ruthless gangster who is unstoppable. They make each other well aware that Baththa has a lion as his pet and how he broke out of a jail with sheer physical strength. This myth making sets the essential ground which the movie deconstructs eventually.  
 Sai Prithviraj plays the character of Sabari, a third-grader who assumes himself to be opposite to what Baththa stands for in his ‘make-believe’ world and does what he has to do to ‘protect’ himself and his family. The unusual aspect about the movie was that Makkal Selvan has been often overshadowed here by young Sabari’s performance, the credit for which goes to the writing which foregrounds the boy’s pov. The movie offers hope and shows how a big shot like Baththa, whose ego and need for one-upmanship seem unshakeable, isn't immune to the simple innocence and honesty of a child—or to the quiet possibility of change. His wrongdoings and holding on to the hegemonic masculinity has haunted him from time to time and when he gets a second chance he does not throw it away. The confrontation scene and the conversation that follows in the movie works well due to its simplicity and approach, and the performances can make the audience shed a tear or two. These emotional scenes when paired with Sai Abhyankar’s music proves a treat for the audience. Although Sai got criticism for his famous “Oorum Blood” Tracks in Dude , here he is praised for the different shades of the song “Magale”, a track which has a role to fulfill in the film’s diegetic space.  
 Overall, Baththa is a comfort watch from the Kollywood industry whose releases are delivering back-to-back praise from the audience these days.
